opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the really interesting things we've discovered is that even very young children are doing something that looks a lot like experimentation, and it's doing real work for them in changing what they believe. When you watch a toddler, what looks like just messing around (dropping the spoon off the high chair for the fifteenth time, pushing the buttons on a toy in every possible combination) turns out to be quite systematic. In our studies, when kids see evidence that's confounded or ambiguous, they play more, and they play in exactly the ways that would help them disambiguate the hypotheses. So "play" is really a kind of exploratory experimentation.

And the reason that matters for theory change is this. If you only learn from passively observing the data that happens to come your way, you're going to be stuck with whatever the statistics of your environment are. You'll see correlations, but you won't be able to tell what's causing what. When you intervene on the world, when you actually do something and see what happens, you get a fundamentally different kind of information. That's the insight from the causal Bayes net work by people like Judea Pearl and Clark Glymour: interventions let you distinguish causal structures that look identical observationally. And it turns out children seem to be sensitive to that difference. They learn differently from their own actions than they do from just watching.

The other piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that experimentation lets you get out of a local optimum. If you're a good Bayesian and you've got a pretty good theory, you'll tend to just keep confirming it. You need some way of trying out things that are a little bit crazy, actions that don't seem to make sense given what you currently believe, in order to find out that there's a better theory out there. Children are wonderful at that. They're noisy, they're variable, they do weird things. From an adult point of view that looks like a bug, but it's really a feature. It's what lets them search a much wider space of hypotheses.

So there's a kind of division of labor across the life span. Childhood is this protected period of exploration, of experimentation, where you can try things out without much cost because someone else is taking care of you. And adulthood is more about exploitation, about using what you've learned to act effectively. Scientists, in a sense, are people who've managed to hold onto some of that childhood exploratory capacity, with a whole institutional apparatus built around them to make that possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses experimentation by children and scientists but does not identify a lack of good accounts of how scientific experiments are conducted.

r002.rationale: It describes children responding to confounded or ambiguous evidence with targeted exploratory play, and explains that interventions provide information that can change beliefs and theories.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that experimentation isn't something that only scientists do. One of the things we've found over and over in the lab is that even very young children, two- and three-year-olds, are actively intervening on the world to figure out how it works. They're not just passively observing and tallying up correlations. When a child picks up a new toy and shakes it and bangs it and pushes the button, that looks like play, and it is play, but it's also a very systematic way of generating evidence that you couldn't get just by watching.

And the reason that matters for theory change is that observation alone is often ambiguous. If you just see that A goes with B, you don't know whether A causes B, or B causes A, or there's some third thing behind both. Intervening breaks that ambiguity. You actually make A happen and see what follows. Children seem to be sensitive to that difference. We've done studies where kids will choose to intervene on exactly the variable that would disambiguate between two hypotheses, and they do that more when the evidence is confusing than when it's clear.

So my view, and this is really the old "child as scientist" idea that Andrew Meltzoff and I and others have been pushing for a long time, is that experimentation is the engine of theory revision. You start with a theory, the theory makes predictions, you act on the world, and when the world surprises you, that's the signal that something in the theory has to give. What's striking is how much children tolerate being wrong. They're not invested in the current theory the way adults, or grown-up scientists for that matter, often are. They have this very exploratory, high-temperature search going on, where they'll try out lots of possibilities, many of which look silly, before settling on one. Adults are more exploitative. We've already got a theory that works well enough, and we're reluctant to tear it up.

And I'd add that I think the formal scientific experiment, with the controls and the randomization, is really just a cultural refinement of something that's deeply built into how human beings learn in the first place. It's the same basic cognitive move, just made more rigorous and more public.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify a lack of good accounts of how to conduct scientific experiments.

r002.rationale: It says people intervene on the world to investigate evidence, and that surprises from acting on the world signal that a theory must change.

astra-6.text:
I think experimentation is crucial because it lets us distinguish between different explanations of the same thing. If you’re just observing the world, you can often come up with several theories that fit what you see. But if you intervene—if you actually change something and see what happens—you can get evidence that separates those theories.

One of the interesting things about children is that they do this spontaneously. What looks to an adult like a child just fiddling around with something can actually be a very informative sequence of experiments. What happens if I push this? What happens if I push that instead? They’re not necessarily articulating a hypothesis, but their actions can give them exactly the evidence they need to revise their understanding.

And there’s a reciprocal relationship: Your theory shapes which experiments you try, and then the results of those experiments can change your theory. So learning isn’t simply accumulating more observations. It’s actively finding ways to make the world tell you something you didn’t already know.

r002.rationale: It says interventions can distinguish explanations and change theories, but does not connect those interventions to investigating surprising observations.

sol-6.1.text:
Experimentation matters because it lets us distinguish between explanations that would otherwise fit the same observations. If you just watch what happens, you may see that two things go together. But when you intervene—change one thing and see what happens to another—you can begin to work out the causal structure of the world.

Children do this all the time. They try something, watch the result, and then try a variation. What looks like pointless play can actually be a very effective way of discovering that their initial picture was wrong. And often the most informative experiment is one whose outcome surprises you.

But there’s a tension here. You need a theory to tell you what would be an interesting experiment, and you need experiments to tell you how to change your theory. So it’s a continuing back-and-forth between imagining possibilities and getting the world to answer you.

r001.rationale: The response explains how experimentation works, but does not identify a lack of good accounts of how to conduct scientific experiments.

r002.rationale: It says interventions help reveal causal structure, that surprising experimental outcomes are especially informative, and that experiments can show an initial picture was wrong.
